title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
Where we left off
\[T_e = \left[\frac{S_0(1-\alpha)}{4\sigma}\right]^{1/4} = 255\ \mathrm{K} \qquad \text{but the surface is } 288\ \mathrm{K}\]

The 255 K is real — satellites measure Earth radiating to space at exactly this temperature
So the question isn’t “why is our formula wrong” — it’s “why is the surface warmer than the planet’s radiation to space?”


5 min. Gently cold-call: “someone reconstruct last week’s logic for us?” A year post-GR5001 + one week post-lecture — expect partial recall, rebuild it fast. Check-in: Lab 0 status by show of hands; due before next class!

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Today: close the gap in four steps
text:
Today: close the gap in four steps

Why the atmosphere intervenes (selective absorption)
The simplest greenhouse (one pane of glass — on the board)
The picture professionals use (emission height)
The 125-year-old objection — and how you will break it


Promise the payoff up front: “by 12:40 you can defeat an argument that fooled physicists for 40 years.”

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Two streams of light that barely touch
text:
Two streams of light that barely touch


Sun (5800 K): peaks near 0.5 µm — shortwave
Earth (255–288 K): peaks near 10–15 µm — longwave
Almost no overlap → energy in and energy out are separate bookkeeping


This spectral separation is a gift — it’s why “solar in, infrared out” is a clean split and why the whole subject is tractable. GR5001 callback: they saw the Trenberth-style budget diagram; this is the physics under its two-column layout.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
Who absorbs what


N₂ + O₂ = ~99% of the air — and nearly transparent in the infrared
The absorbers are the vibrating, polar trace molecules: H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, O₃, N₂O
Nearly transparent at 0.5 µm, strongly absorbing at 10–15 µm


One sentence of molecular physics is enough: symmetric diatomic molecules have no dipole moment to grab infrared photons; triatomic benders and stretchers do. Don’t go deeper unless asked.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: The greenhouse effect is a trace-gas effect
text:
The greenhouse effect is a trace-gas effect

“CO₂ is only 0.04% of the atmosphere!”


Correct — and that 0.04% (plus water vapor) is doing all of the work. Remove every trace gas and keep the 99%: Earth freezes.

Reframe the talking point as the actual story. Plant (don’t fully develop) the week-9 distinction: H₂O is the biggest absorber, but it condenses — days of residence, slaved to temperature — so it’s a feedback, an amplifier. CO₂ is the forcing, the control knob. Lacis et al. 2010 ran it: remove CO₂, the water vapor rains out, Earth ices over. Full treatment Nov 5.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
The simplest greenhouse: setup
One atmospheric layer that is:

transparent to shortwave (sunlight passes through)
perfectly absorbing in longwave (nothing gets past it)
radiating \(\sigma T_a^4\) both up and down



BOARD, not slides, for the whole derivation (~15 min). Two budgets, two unknowns — ask the room to supply each term before writing it. This is the second board derivation of the course (after week 1’s T_e); same culture: they follow, not admire.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
The derivation (record)
Top of atmosphere: what leaves = what enters \[\sigma T_a^4 = \tfrac{S_0}{4}(1-\alpha) \;\Rightarrow\; T_a = T_e = 255\ \mathrm{K}\]
Surface: heated by Sun and by the sky \[\sigma T_s^4 = \tfrac{S_0}{4}(1-\alpha) + \sigma T_a^4 \;\Rightarrow\; T_s = 2^{1/4}\,T_e \approx 303\ \mathrm{K}\]

Pause on what fell out: the ATMOSPHERE sits at the emission temperature; the surface is warmer than both. The layer doesn’t “trap” heat — it re-radiates downward. Kill the blanket metaphor here (blankets suppress convection; Wood’s 1909 rock-salt greenhouse experiment if asked).

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Three surprises from one tiny model
text:
Three surprises from one tiny model

The atmosphere radiates at 255 K — the surface hides beneath it, warmer
The surface receives more energy from the sky than from the Sun (~340 vs ~168 W/m² in the real budget)
It overshoots: 303 K predicted vs 288 K observed


#2 is the intuition-breaker — let it sit. It’s in the observed surface budget (GR5001’s diagram!): downwelling longwave beats absorbed solar at the ground. #3 is the productive failure that drives the next slide.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Why the overshoot? The best kind of wrong
text:
Why the overshoot? The best kind of wrong

The real atmosphere isn’t a perfect absorber (windows, wings)
Deeper: convection short-circuits radiation — ~100 W/m² leaves the surface as evaporation + thermals, not photons
Pure radiative equilibrium would make the lower atmosphere absurdly steep and unstable → convection overturns it and pins the lapse rate ≈ 6.5 K/km


Automating exactly this repair = Manabe & Wetherald 1967 (week 1’s “most influential paper”).

This is the week’s 5-minute vertical-structure aside — the ONLY dose of RCE this week (thread returns Nov 5). GR5001 callback: their week 3 was convection; “you know why air rises — here’s what that does to the greenhouse.” M&W Fig 16 from last week can reappear for one beat.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Where does Earth’s radiation to space really come from?
text:
Where does Earth’s radiation to space really come from?
In the CO₂/H₂O bands the atmosphere is optically thick: surface photons are absorbed and re-emitted many times before escaping.
Effectively, space “sees” radiation not from the ground but from an effective emission height:
\[z_e \approx 5\text{–}6\ \mathrm{km}, \quad \text{where } T \approx 255\ \mathrm{K}\]


Connect back: the 255 K from week 1 is REAL — satellites measure it. This slide says where it lives: ~5.5 km up. The layer model was a cartoon of this.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Add CO₂ → the radiating surface rises
text:
Add CO₂ → the radiating surface rises

More CO₂ → atmosphere more opaque in the IR → z_e rises
Higher = colder (lapse rate!) → planet radiates less to space
Energy imbalance → the whole column warms…
…until the new emission height is back at 255 K
The surface, ~6 km below along the lapse rate, ends up warmer

\[\Delta T_s \approx \Gamma \cdot \Delta z_e \qquad (\sim150\ \mathrm{m\ rise} \approx 1\ \mathrm{K})\]

Walk the 5 steps slowly, twice if needed — this is the mental model to install for the whole course. Note what restores balance: not the surface “trapping” anything, but the planet’s radiating level sliding up a fixed temperature ladder.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
One sentence to keep

Global warming = raising the height from which Earth radiates to space — with the surface dragged warmer along the lapse rate.


Say it, let them write it, move on. This sentence defeats arguments the layer model can’t (next block).

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
This picture makes free predictions

The stratosphere should cool as the surface warms (it sits above the emission level) — observed ✓, and a fingerprint pure solar warming would not produce
No lapse rate → no warming from raising \(z_e\) → the lapse rate itself matters (week 9: lapse-rate feedback)


Stratospheric cooling: predicted by M&W 1967 (they saw it in Fig 16 last week), confirmed decades later by satellites/radiosondes. This is the honest counterweight to “models are tuned” — fingerprint predictions made before the observations existed.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
1900: Ångström vs Arrhenius

“The CO₂ absorption band is already saturated — the center of the 15 µm band absorbs everything within meters. Adding more CO₂ can’t do anything.” — Knut Ångström’s lab assistant, 1900 (paraphrased)

This argument killed interest in Arrhenius’s work for decades. It still circulates today.
By the end of this hour, you’ll be able to break it. (That’s literally the next activity.)

Frame it with respect — it’s a GOOD objection, and the physics community bought it for ~40 years. Don’t reveal the answer yet.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
Look at the actual spectrum


Band center: opaque at 280 ppm, opaque at 560 ppm — Ångström was right about the center
Band wings: visibly deepening — this is where doubling acts


LIVE DEMO if wifi cooperates (U. Chicago MODTRAN, ~8 min): set 280 ppm, note outgoing flux; double to 560; the flux drops ~3 W/m²; zoom the band wings. Students see the forcing in measured-quantity space. Screenshots on this slide are the wifi-failure fallback — rehearse the demo once beforehand.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Why the response is a logarithm (not zero)
text:
Why the response is a logarithm (not zero)
Each doubling widens the effective opaque interval by roughly the same spectral increment:
\[\Delta F \approx 5.35 \cdot \ln\!\left(\frac{C}{C_0}\right)\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} \qquad \approx 3.7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\ per\ doubling}\]

Saturation is why it’s a log — not why it’s zero
This is why climate speaks in doublings, and why ECS is defined per doubling


280→560 ppm and 560→1120 ppm have the SAME forcing. Also note: this one-line formula is how CMIP-model forcings are quoted and compared — the toy is the ruler (bridge beat returns at the end).

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
Your turn: break Ångström (pairs, ~12 min)
Here is the argument, verbatim:

“The CO₂ band is already saturated — the atmosphere absorbs all the radiation in that band within a few hundred meters. More CO₂ cannot change the energy balance.”

With your partner, write the strongest 3–4 sentence rebuttal you can. Use anything from today. Names on the slip; hand it in.

Circulate with the TAs. Most pairs will find the wings; the deeper rebuttal (emission height rises regardless — a saturated band just means z_e is HIGH, not that it can’t go higher) is what the debrief adds. Slips → participation credit.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Debrief: three independent ways it fails
text:
Debrief: three independent ways it fails

The wings aren’t saturated — and that’s where doubling acts (you saw it in the spectrum)
The emission height rises regardless — saturation means \(z_e\) is high, not that it’s stuck; higher is colder is less radiation
Thin, cold upper layers always radiate less — there is no altitude where “more absorber” stops mattering


Argument 2 is the professional one — flag that pairs who found it were reasoning at the research level. Historical coda, 1 sentence: the 1940s–50s spectroscopy (partly military-funded, Plass et al.) resolved the band structure and revived CO₂ science.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Scale-up: radiation in a real climate model
text:
Scale-up: radiation in a real climate model

Line-by-line absorption: physically exact, computationally hopeless at runtime
Models use band schemes (“correlated-k”), validated against line-by-line codes
Radiation is computed in every column, ~100 levels, every 1–3 model hours


Your layer model and a GCM’s radiation code differ in resolution, not in kind.

The point of the scale-up beat every week: demystify. The radiation module of a CMIP model is the N-layer model with real spectroscopy and clever bookkeeping.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Bridge: the toy is the ruler
text:
Bridge: the toy is the ruler

Backward: Manabe & Wetherald 1967 = today’s chain done right the first time — real spectra + convection-pinned lapse rate → ECS ≈ 2.3 K, within today’s assessed range
Forward: when CMIP models are compared, their CO₂ forcing is quoted through the same \(5.35\ln(C/C_0)\) — the formula you now own


Close the loop explicitly — this is the weekly bridge sentence: “the simple model isn’t a stepping stone we discard; it’s the instrument the community measures the big models with.” Next week’s bridge is even stronger (their lab EBM is literally fit to every CMIP model).

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text: Earth system and climate models are critically important tools for climate science — used to study past climate variability, attribute recent trends and extremes, and project the evolution of the climate system under natural and anthropogenic forcing. This course opens the machine: you will build the hierarchy of climate models yourself in Python, understand how full Earth System Models work, analyze their output (CMIP6) the way practicing scientists do, and learn to judge what models can and cannot tell you.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: Before we start: three hands-up questions
text:
Before we start: three hands-up questions

Roughly what sets the Earth’s average temperature? (could you explain it to a friend?)
Have you written Python this year?
Do you remember what “climate sensitivity” means?


Ungraded diagnostic — calibrates refresher dosage for weeks 2–9. Framing: “a year since GR5001 is a long time; that’s expected.”

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: Every number on this figure came out of a model
text:
Every number on this figure came out of a model


The hook. “Sea level in 2100, warming under net-zero — every quantitative claim about the climate future is a model output. This course is about whether — and when, and how much — to believe them.”

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: The question someone is already thinking
text:
The question someone is already thinking

“Aren’t these models just tuned to give the answer the modelers expect?”


A real question — asked inside the field too. November 12 is a full session on it.
And in the next 40 minutes, you’ll see the honest shape of the answer — using a bucket.

Raise it proactively, don’t answer beyond one sentence. The bucket demo’s ending (“no box to open”) IS the shape of the answer — say so when you get there.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
The rules of the game

I have a system: water flows in (with some “weather” in it), the level responds
I’ve measured inflow and level for a long time — you get the data
I will not tell you what’s inside
Your job: a simpler description good enough to predict situations we haven’t seen


That’s modeling. That’s also this entire course, in one sitting.

Before the models: pause on the raw data plot and name the concepts (next slide).

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: The bucket has weather — and a climate
text:
The bucket has weather — and a climate

The level wiggles constantly (noisy tap) — that’s its weather
But its statistics are steady: mean ≈ 1, a typical spread, a typical excursion time — that’s its climate


Climate = the statistics of a system. You’ve now defined it — on a bucket. Earth’s version: means, variability, extremes over ~30 years.

Then switch to the notebook (bucket_hierarchy.ipynb) and LIVE-DRIVE it: data → statistical fit → THE COMMITMENT MOMENT (slips of paper: “I double the inflow — what’s the new level? number + reasoning + name”) → regression fails publicly → budget thinking → equilibrium prediction ✓ → time-dependent model ✓ → the storm breaks it → the reveal. ~25 min in the notebook. Collect slips (participation). Do NOT rush the commitment moment — the public stake is what makes the failure memorable.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
What just happened (part 1)

A model = a simpler description of a complicated system, built for a purpose
Statistical models are real models — but they interpolate; change the system and they fail (week 13: remember this about AI)
Budgets — in − out = accumulation — are where physical modeling starts
Equilibrium budgets already predict a lot (and found the nonlinearity the line couldn’t)

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
What just happened (part 2)

Time dependence = lags + adjustment, governed by a stabilizing feedback (fuller → drains harder)
Even physical models are calibrated — we fitted \(k\); we lived with the evaporation bias (week 10 is entirely about this)
Every model has a regime of validity — discovered, usually, the hard way
Different questions → different models: average level vs. flood timing. “Best” depends on the question


Read these fast — they just witnessed each one; the slides are the receipt. #8 replaces the old card-sort’s job.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
One more thing — the thing
Today, when our models failed, we opened the box and checked.

For the Earth, there is no box to open.
No spare planet, no truth-generator to read. Everything climate science knows about 2100 comes from models earning trust the way ours did today: predicting things they weren’t fitted to.

Let this land in silence for a beat. It’s the epistemological heart of the course and the honest answer to the tuning question raised in the hook. Optional aside: climate scientists simulate today’s luxury deliberately — “perfect-model experiments,” using one GCM as fake truth to test methods.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: This course = that exercise, for Earth
text:
This course = that exercise, for Earth
Last year GR5001 taught you what the climate system does. This course opens the machine that predicts it:

Build the model hierarchy yourselves, in Python (weeks 1–8)
Understand feedbacks, sensitivity, tuning — can we trust this? (weeks 9–10)
Analyze the real models’ output the way scientists do — CMIP6 (weeks 11–13)
Answer your own question with model data (final project)


~5 min. The four acts, now motivated by the demo instead of asserted. By December: built models, run CMIP6 analyses, a research project, and an informed answer to the tuning question.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: 1896: Arrhenius computes the climate by hand
text:
1896: Arrhenius computes the climate by hand


Motivated by ice ages, not fossil fuels
Months of hand calculation: a radiative budget + water-vapor amplification
His CO₂-doubling answer: ~5–6 °C (modern: 2.5–4 °C) — high, but the structure is modern
He was doing exactly our Model 1: an equilibrium budget


~50 min total for the history segment — it’s tightened; keep moving. Color: 1908 he guessed warming would take millennia and be pleasant → why nobody panicked. Callendar 1938 (station data, dismissed) in one breath. Tease: “we’ll do Arrhenius’s first step ourselves before you leave.”

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
1922: Richardson’s magnificent failure


Hand-integrated the fluid equations for a 6-hour forecast: absurdly wrong
But grid + finite differences + timestepping = exactly what every model does today
His failure: too-honest equations amplified noisy data


The forecast factory is a parallel supercomputer, 80 years early (week 5 callback). Bridge to next slide: the fix wasn’t a bigger machine.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: 1950: ENIAC — a smarter simple model wins
text:
1950: ENIAC — a smarter simple model wins
Charney, Fjørtoft & von Neumann: first numerical forecast — by simplifying (one quasi-geostrophic level filtered out Richardson’s noise).

Weather vs climate: forecast = initial-value problem (chaos kills it in ~2 weeks); climate = boundary-value problem (statistics under a push).

The casino: no one predicts the next hand. The house margin is a certainty.


Two beats on one slide to save time: the thesis anecdote + THE misconception-killer. If pressed on “but chaos!”: forced response vs internal variability — the bucket’s level statistics under doubled inflow were predictable even though its wiggles weren’t.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
1956–1975: columns, spheres, coupling

Phillips 1956: two-level hemisphere → jets emerged, uncoded — put conservation on a grid and circulation is what balance looks like
Manabe & Wetherald 1967: the 1-D column done right — ECS ≈ 2.3 °C; predicted stratospheric cooling (observed decades later); voted most influential climate paper ever
Manabe & Bryan 1969: ocean coupled · M&W 1975: first 3-D CO₂ doubling → polar amplification predicted



Compressed from three slides. Manabe from Tokyo to GFDL 1958; “get one column right before the sphere.” Fingerprint predictions made before observations = honest counterweight to the tuning worry.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: 1979 → 2021: the error bar and the enterprise
text:
1979 → 2021: the error bar and the enterprise

Charney Report 1979 (two GCMs on Earth): ECS = 1.5–4.5 °C → AR6 2021: 2.5–4 °C. 42 years to halve the bar — why so slow? (Nov 5.)
CMIP (1995→): every center runs the same experiments — model spread becomes data
GCMs absorb carbon, chemistry, ice → Earth System Models

“Which model is best?” is meaningless without “…for what question?” — you proved this with a bucket an hour ago.

text:
The first calculation (live, on the board)
Energy in: sunlight on a disk — \(\pi R^2 S_0(1-\alpha)\). Energy out: infrared from a sphere — \(4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4\).
\[T_e = \left[\frac{S_0(1-\alpha)}{4\sigma}\right]^{1/4} \approx \mathbf{255\ K} = -18\,°\mathrm{C}\;\;(?!)\]




formula
actual




Mars
~210 K
~218 K ✓


Earth
255 K
288 K — off by 33 K


Venus
~230 K
735 K — off by 500 K!




Board derivation, slowly — ask “why πR² in but 4πR² out?” before answering; sets the math culture. This is Arrhenius’s step 1, and our Model-1 equilibrium budget for the planet. Venus kills “it’s distance from the Sun.” In Lab 0 this week they plot exactly this formula.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: 33 K — the most productive wrong answer in science
text:
33 K — the most productive wrong answer in science
That gap is the greenhouse effect. Closing it:

Week 2: why — the layer model + the picture professionals use
Week 3: when — the model ticks in time; the ocean sets the clock
Week 9: how much — feedbacks decide whether 3.7 W/m² means 2 °C or 5 °C


Honest note: 255 K is REAL — satellites measure Earth radiating at exactly this temperature. The puzzle is precise. Cliffhanger, then logistics.
